# Judges Chapter 16 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-09

---

### v.16 — "his soul was vexed to death" vs. "he was sick to death of it"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "his soul was shortened to death" | vatiqtsar nafsho lamut — literal |
| LOGOS | "his soul was vexed to death" | Interprets qatsar nefesh as vexation |
| PNEUMA | "he was sick to death of it" | Modern English idiom |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew vatiqtsar nafsho lamut uses the same idiom as 10:16 (God's soul "shortened" over Israel's misery). EMET's literal rendering preserves the verbal parallel but is opaque. LOGOS's "vexed to death" captures the sense — Samson is worn down beyond endurance. PNEUMA's "sick to death of it" is colloquial and loses the literary connection to 10:16.

**Status:** Moderate. Same idiom as 10:16 — the parallel between God's exasperation and Samson's is narratively significant.

---

### v.25 — "entertained them" vs. "was being made an object of ridicule"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "he amused before them" | vay'tsacheq liphnehem — from tsachaq, "to play/laugh/amuse" |
| LOGOS | "he entertained them" | Same |
| PNEUMA | "Samson was being made an object of ridicule" | Interprets entertainment as humiliation |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew tsachaq means "to play/laugh/sport/amuse" — the same verb used of Isaac's name ("he laughs") and of the golden calf incident ("they rose up to play," Exodus 32:6). The text says Samson "played/performed" before them. PNEUMA's "made an object of ridicule" is interpretively correct — the performance is humiliating — but the Hebrew verb itself is neutral. The humiliation is in the context, not the verb. The text's restraint allows the reader to feel the horror without being told to.

**Status:** Minor. Narrative tone — showing vs. telling.

---

### v.28 — "that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes" vs. "let me pay back the Philistines for the loss of my two eyes"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "let me be avenged with one vengeance for my two eyes from the P'lishtim" | niqmat-achat mishshetei einai — literal |
| LOGOS | "that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes" | Formal |
| PNEUMA | "With one blow let me pay back the Philistines for the loss of my two eyes" | Dynamic, adds "with one blow" |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted LOGOS. The Hebrew specifies "one vengeance for my two eyes" — the numerical contrast (one/two) is deliberate. PNEUMA adds "with one blow" which is not in the text and shifts the emphasis from the theological irony (one vengeance for two eyes) to the physical action.

**Status:** Minor. Numerical precision in the Hebrew.

---

## Summary of Disagreement Patterns

| Pattern | Count | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Key idiom parallel | 1 | qatsar nefesh — connects Samson to God (v.16 / 10:16) |
| PNEUMA interprets neutral verb | 1 | tsachaq "entertained" → "made an object of ridicule" (v.25) |
| PNEUMA adds to text | 1 | "With one blow" not in Hebrew (v.28) |

**Overall pattern:** Chapter 16 produces relatively few disagreements for such a famous passage. The most significant is v.16 — the qatsar nefesh idiom that verbally links Samson's exasperation with God's exasperation in 10:16. PNEUMA's colloquial rendering breaks this connection.

---

*— SOPHIA, AI Translator, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
